source: Jones & Harris (1967) The attribution of attitudes, as described in Norenzayan & Nisbett (2000) Culture and causal cognition
finding: Classic correspondence-bias paradigm. Readers saw an essay or speech (for example on legalising marijuana, or on Castro) that a target was told by a debate coach or experimenter to write. Readers still inferred the target held the view in the essay.
numbers: No N or effect size given in the review. Wikipedia summary (opened) adds: pro-Castro writers rated more pro-Castro even when told the position was set by coin toss.
quote: participants' estimates of the target's actual views reflected to a substantial extent the views expressed in the speech or essay, even when they knew that the target had been explicitly instructed
limits: Secondary description only; original not opened. Later work (Malle 2006, via Wikipedia) says one form of the FAE lacks support.
agent_relevance: A reasoning scaffold should force an explicit check: was the stated view assigned or chosen? Models can repeat the same slip.

source: Ross (1977) the intuitive psychologist and the fundamental attribution error, as described in Norenzayan & Nisbett (2000) Culture and causal cognition
finding: Ross named the fundamental attribution error (FAE): the habit of seeing behaviour as caused by matching dispositions even when obvious situational constraints leave little role for dispositions.
numbers: No numbers in the source.
quote: the FAE ... until recently was held to be invariable across cultures
limits: Name and scope of FAE disputed; Gilbert & Malone prefer the term correspondence bias. Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Defines the target error that a guardrail on blame or cause claims would need to catch.

source: Wikipedia (2026) Fundamental attribution error
finding: Review page gives the standard story and the critiques. Malle (2006) meta-analysis found little support for actor-observer asymmetry and for the first form of the FAE; the second form (inferring stable dispositions from one situation) is not contradicted. Walker, Smith and Vul (2015) say the bias looks like error only against a wrong rationality benchmark.
numbers: No sample sizes on the page. Cultural claim: individualist cultures reportedly more prone; Hindu children in India used more situational factors than US children.
quote: the existing weight of evidence does not support the first form of the fundamental attribution error
limits: Encyclopedia page, not primary. Numbers must be taken from the originals.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code FAE as a universal flaw; treat it as a conditional bias with a stated benchmark.

source: Wikipedia (2026) Attribution (psychology)
finding: Lists the founding theories. Heider 1958: internal vs external causes; ability, effort, task difficulty. Kelley 1967 covariation: consensus, distinctiveness, consistency. Jones & Davis correspondent inference: choice, expectedness, effects. Weiner: locus, stability, controllability. Jones & Nisbett 1971: actor-observer difference.
numbers: No statistics on the page.
limits: Encyclopedia page; McArthur 1972 not covered. Page flags possible original research in the actor-observer section.
agent_relevance: Kelley's three covariation cues are a ready, checkable template for any 'why did this happen' step.

source: Bohm & Pfister (2015) How people explain their own and others' behavior: a theory of lay causal explanations
finding: Model of lay causal explanation with seven categories (goals, dispositions, temporary states, intentional actions, outcomes, events, stimulus attributes) and inference rules: actions caused by goals; goals by higher goals or states; states by dispositions, stimulus attributes or events; events by dispositions or earlier events.
numbers: Two experiments: Exp 1 free-response explanations followed the rules (multidimensional scaling of similarity judgments); Exp 2 matching explanations were generated faster and more often. Exact N not extracted.
quote: different types of behavior trigger different hypotheses concerning the types of causes
limits: Person-vs-situation split is too coarse; specific goals and motives predict dispositional inference better (Reeder et al. 2004, cited). Western samples.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to a formal causal-typing rule set; could inform an explanation-typing operator.

source: Morris & Peng (1994) Culture and cause, fish animation, as described in Mason & Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity
finding: Morris and Peng adapted Heider-Simmel animations with a fish swimming relative to a group. Chinese perceivers leaned toward situational cause (the group); Americans toward the fish's own dispositions. No such difference for physical events (circle and rectangle).
numbers: No N or effect size in the review.
limits: Secondary description; the Berkeley PDF of the original did not download. Differences appeared for social, not physical, events.
agent_relevance: Cultural cause-attribution style may live in training text; prompts in different languages could shift model attributions.

source: Morris & Peng (1994) newspaper study, as described in Norenzayan & Nisbett (2000) Culture and causal cognition
finding: Chinese newspapers and Chinese students in the US explained murders (by Chinese or American perpetrators) with situations and societal context. American papers and students used presumed dispositions of the perpetrator.
numbers: No counts in this source.
limits: Secondary; correlational on media. Reporter culture mattered, perpetrator nationality did not.
agent_relevance: Culture of the text source shapes causal framing; relevant to LLMs trained on mixed-language corpora.

source: Choi, Nisbett & Norenzayan (1999) Jones-Harris replication with Koreans and Americans, as described in Norenzayan & Nisbett (2000) Culture and causal cognition
finding: Koreans, like Americans, inferred the target held the position he advocated. When observers first wrote the constrained essay themselves, Americans were unaffected but Koreans almost never inferred the attitude.
numbers: No N in the review. Qualitative: Americans unchanged by experiencing the constraint; Koreans greatly affected.
quote: the Americans were unaffected, but the Koreans were greatly affected
limits: Correspondence bias occurs across cultures; the difference is sensitivity to situational salience. Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the cultural gap shrinks when situational cues are not salient. Salience of constraints in the prompt matters.

source: Choi & Nisbett (1998) situational salience, as described in Mason & Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity
finding: When evidence for situational causation was made stronger (essay closely echoed the experimenter's instructions), Koreans' correspondence bias decreased. Americans' did not.
numbers: No N or effect sizes in the review.
limits: Review summary only; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Americans' insensitivity to stronger constraint evidence mirrors a model that ignores context cues.

source: Miyamoto & Kitayama (2002) attitude diagnosticity, as described in Mason & Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity
finding: When the essay was made less compelling (more believably forced by the situation), dispositional inferences fell for Japanese but not American perceivers. Supports the attitude-diagnosticity account.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Review summary only.
agent_relevance: Suggests correction depends on how diagnostic the behaviour is believed to be, a quantity an agent could estimate.

source: Masuda & Kitayama (2004) as described in Mason & Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity
finding: Standard no-choice condition produced attitude attributions in both Americans and Japanese. Under strong situational constraint, Japanese correspondence bias fell, American did not. Situational manipulation worked more when attentional resources were free.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Review summary; attention-load effects found in both groups.
agent_relevance: Attention (compute or context budget) trades off against situational correction.

source: Gilbert, Pelham & Krull (1988) anchoring-and-adjustment, as described in Mason & Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity
finding: Two-stage account: people anchor on a dispositional inference then adjust for the situation. Under attentional load, adjustment fails. Participants judged a woman's trait anxiety from a silent video with stressful or nonstressful topic information.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Review says the evidence for the two-stage framework is 'remarkably thin'. Krull 1993: situational-goal perceivers also failed to discount under load.
agent_relevance: A computational model: fast anchor plus effortful correction. Maps to cheap first pass then explicit check.

source: Knowles et al. (2001) as described in Mason & Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity
finding: US and Hong Kong students heard a speech on an unpopular political position, with load and constraint manipulated. Hong Kong perceivers' situational correction was not disrupted by load, consistent with automatised situational adjustment.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Review summary. Alternative: Easterners may hold a chronic situational inference goal.
agent_relevance: Two rival explanations (automatic correction vs different default goal). Both predict that goal framing in the prompt matters.

source: Lieberman et al. (2005) as described in Mason & Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity
finding: Anxious-interview paradigm with US students and East Asian foreign students. Under load, both groups imputed stressful topics similarly. Under low load the groups diverged: US students became less confident in situational attribution, East Asians more confident.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Review summary only.
agent_relevance: The cultural gap appears in the controlled stage.

source: Hedden et al. (2008) fMRI, as described in Mason & Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity
finding: Participants judging under conditions that conflict with their culture's approach showed more activation in controlled-processing regions (DLPFC); conditions matching their culture did not.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Review summary; neural claims rest on reverse inference.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Mason & Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity
finding: Reviews whether cultural differences in attribution lie in automatic or controlled components. Sets anchoring-adjustment vs more-automatized-correction vs different-inferential-goal accounts against each other. Concludes the evidence for a two-stage model is thin.
numbers: Review; no pooled effect sizes.
quote: the evidence for it is remarkably thin
limits: Review, mostly Western and East Asian students.
agent_relevance: Gives the rival explanations to test: perception, goal, folk theory, automaticity.

source: Norenzayan & Nisbett (2000) Culture and causal cognition
finding: Short review of cultural attribution. East Asians see behaviour as an interaction of dispositions and context; Americans as direct unfolding of dispositions. When situational cues are not salient, Asians rely on dispositions or show the FAE as much as Westerners.
numbers: Norenzayan, Choi & Nisbett (1999): Koreans and Americans endorsed the dispositionist philosophy equally; Koreans endorsed situationist and interactionist views more. Koreans mostly rejected entity theory; Americans split evenly between entity and incremental.
quote: the cultural difference seems to originate primarily from a stronger East Asian tendency to recognize the causal power of situations
limits: Four-page review; no sample sizes. The Greek vs Chinese intellectual-history explanation is called highly speculative by the authors.
agent_relevance: Frames the gap as folk-theory difference, not capacity difference; so prompt framing, not model size, should move attributions.

source: Peng & Nisbett physical-event studies, as described in Norenzayan & Nisbett (2000) Culture and causal cognition
finding: Chinese participants read ambiguous schematic physical events (an object dropping through a surface and returning) as due to the relation with a medium such as water. Americans read them as due to the object's own properties.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Review summary; Nisbett et al. 2001 itself was not opened (HTTP 403).
agent_relevance: Holistic vs analytic causal style extends beyond persons.

source: Masuda & Nisbett (2001) fish scene recall, as described in Norenzayan & Nisbett (2000) Culture and causal cognition
finding: Japanese and Americans viewed underwater scenes with focal fish. Both recalled equal detail on focal fish. Japanese recalled far more about everything else.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Review summary.
agent_relevance: Supports an attention-to-field mechanism for context-heavy attribution.

source: Talhelm et al. (2025) New evidence finds young people in Mainland China are now bicultural (Study 1, Hong Kong)
finding: Replication of Hong et al. (2000) priming: Hong Kong students primed with American images gave more internal attributions than those primed with Chinese images.
numbers: N=107 (df 104). F(2,104)=20.23, f2=.388. Means (1-5 internal): American prime 3.24 (SD .37), Chinese prime 2.70 (SD .41), control 3.07 (SD .31). American vs Chinese d=1.479 [0.915, 2.044]; control vs Chinese d=1.012.
limits: Not preregistered. Fish-animation items from Morris and Peng; self-report ratings.
agent_relevance: Large attribution shift from a light prime; prompts could shift LLM attribution style.

source: Talhelm et al. (2025) New evidence finds young people in Mainland China are now bicultural (Study 2, mainland college students)
finding: Young mainland Chinese students primed with Chinese culture gave more external attributions; primed with American culture gave more internal. Evidence of biculturalism.
numbers: N=272 after excluding 28 of 300. F(2,269)=26.15, f2=.195 [.110,.294]; controlling demographics F(2,264)=13.19, f2=.100.
limits: Online Tencent sample; not preregistered; self-report.
agent_relevance: Effect is smaller than in Study 1 (f2 .195 vs .388).

source: Talhelm et al. (2025) New evidence finds young people in Mainland China are now bicultural (Study 3, older adults negative control)
finding: Chinese adults born before 1978 showed no priming effect on internal attributions, as predicted for a negative control.
numbers: N=258 after excluding 42 of 300. F(2,255)=1.10, p=.335, f2=.009. Means: China prime 2.89, America 3.00, control 2.93. Generation x prime interaction in combined analysis F(2,524)=5.09, p=.006, f2=.019.
limits: Cohort differences are confounded with age. Dialectical self-concept still moved with Chinese priming in this group.
agent_relevance: Cultural attribution style can be switched on by context only if the person holds both schemas.

source: Bott et al. (2022) Spontaneous trait inferences from behavior: a systematic meta-analysis
finding: First meta-analysis of spontaneous trait inference. Average effect moderate to large and robust to publication bias. Cultural background (independent vs interdependent) did not moderate the effect.
numbers: k=86 publications, N=13,630. Average dz=0.59. Culture moderator: independent ES 0.62 [0.54,0.70] (67 records), interdependent ES 0.51 [0.39,0.64] (13 records); beta -0.09 [-0.24, 0.06], chi2(1)=1.39, p=.239.
quote: Contrary to expectations, cultural background (independent vs. interdependent) did not emerge as a significant moderator
limits: Interdependent sample much smaller (13 vs 67 records). Paradigm moderated the effect: larger in long-term-memory than working-memory paradigms. Tests inference, not explicit causal judgments.
agent_relevance: Key counterweight: the automatic dispositional step looks universal; cultural differences sit in later correction.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: Tests 30 biases in 20 LLMs with 30,000 generated tests. FAE is among the weaker biases. FAE test uses an actor-observer perspective (second- vs third-person pronouns), following Flick & Schweitzer 2021, Hooper 2015, Riggio & Garcia 2009.
numbers: Mean FAE bias score across models 0.10 (per-model range about -0.02 to 0.23). Compare Information Bias 0.54, In-Group Bias 0.41, Framing 0.41. Mean over all biases 0.13.
limits: FAE operationalised by pronoun swap, not the classic attitude-attribution paradigm; no culture manipulation. Models tested around Oct 2024.
agent_relevance: FAE is a small effect in LLMs here; worry more about framing and anchoring.

source: Raj et al. (2026) Talent or Luck? Evaluating Attribution Bias in LLMs
finding: 140k-prompt benchmark of internal (effort, ability) vs external (task difficulty, luck) attributions across ten scenarios and four social dimensions, in three settings: Single-Actor, Actor-Actor, Actor-Observer. Models attribute success to internal and failure to external causes, like the human self-serving pattern.
numbers: Headline models: Aya-Expanse-8B, Qwen-32B, Llama-3.3-70B (plus Llama 3.2-1B and 3.1-8B for size trends). Effect size d with two-sided t-tests at 95% CI. Smaller model leans external; 32B and 70B lean internal.
limits: Only three headline models. Identity effects vary by model and scenario. Exact d values are in figures, not extracted.
agent_relevance: Attribution is identity-sensitive; a fairness guardrail should test attribution swaps across demographic variants.

source: Raj et al. (2026) Talent or Luck? identity findings
finding: Asian, Middle Eastern and Hispanic women got more internal attributions than male counterparts. White and Black males got mostly external attributions. Failures of Russian, French, German, Japanese and Korean actors were more often internalised (harsher). Education, Sports and Workplace success was credited to effort.
numbers: Directional findings from the text; significance marked in figures at 95% CI. No exact d in text.
limits: Descriptive; the authors call some patterns counterintuitive.
agent_relevance: Cross-national attribution asymmetries in models resemble cultural attribution research in form but not necessarily in cause.

source: Talhelm et al. (2025) cultural-attribution background citations
finding: Paper cites East Asians endorsing external attributions more than Westerners (Dean & Koenig 2019; Morris & Peng 1994; Spencer-Rodgers et al. 2012). Hong et al. (2000) bicultural priming extended the finding.
numbers: No numbers beyond the studies above.
limits: Secondary citations; Dean & Koenig chapter and Spencer-Rodgers not opened.
agent_relevance: Leads for later angles.

source: Na, Huang & Park (2017) When age and culture interact in categorization
finding: Adjacent evidence that Asians are more intuitive and Americans more rule-based, the base of analytic-holistic theory. Atypicality cost larger in older adults; Singapore vs US gap only among older adults.
numbers: Young and old Singaporeans and Americans; living vs non-living categorisation; age x culture interaction on RT cost. Exact N not extracted.
limits: Categorisation task, not attribution. Culture effect only in the older group.
agent_relevance: Cultural cognitive-style gaps can be age-bound; not directly about attribution.
